function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

Here’s a quick rundown of the most common ways to get a cake delivered (or pick it up) so you can decide what works best for your situation: | Option | How it Works | Pros | Cons | |--------|--------------|------|------| | **Local bakery website** | Many brick‑and‑mortar bakeries now have their own sites or Facebook pages where you can place an order directly. | • Fresh, often handmade.
• You can see photos, read reviews, and sometimes customize flavors.
• Direct support for small businesses. | • Delivery may be limited to a certain radius.
• Some sites don’t accept credit cards; you might need to call. | | **Online food‑delivery platforms** (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Postmates, Seamless) | Search “cake” or “bakery” in the app; you’ll see a mix of local shops and chain bakeries. | • One‑stop shop for many vendors.
• Real‑time tracking & driver ETA.
• Often free delivery if you meet a minimum spend. | • Delivery fees can add up.
• Not all bakeries are listed; you may miss niche shops. | | **Grocery‑store delivery** (Instacart, Amazon Fresh, Walmart Grocery) | Order from the store’s online catalog; they’ll deliver a pre‑made cake or a cake kit. | • Convenient if you’re already shopping there.
• Usually same‑day delivery. | • Limited selection compared to dedicated bakeries.
• May not offer custom designs. | | **Specialty cake marketplaces** (Etsy, CakeDelivery.com, BakeShare) | Browse artisans who ship nationwide or locally. | • Unique, artisanal designs.
• Ability to communicate directly with the maker. | • Shipping times vary; you need to plan ahead.
• Prices can be higher due to shipping costs. | | **National chains** (Baker’s Dozen, Mrs. Fields, Cinnabon, Panera Bread) | Order through their website or app; they usually have a “specialty items” section. | • Reliable quality standards.
• Nationwide coverage. | • Less variety in flavors/designs.
• Delivery may be slower than local shops. | ### Quick Tips for Ordering 1. **Check Reviews & Photos** Look at recent customer photos on Google Maps, Yelp, or the vendor’s social media. That gives you a realistic idea of the cake’s appearance and taste. 2. **Ask About Customization** If you need a specific flavor, size, or design, call or email the bakery first. Some places only take custom orders over the phone. 3. **Know the Delivery Window** Most platforms show an estimated arrival time. If you need the cake at a particular time (e.g., a birthday), confirm the exact window when placing the order. 4. **Watch Out for Fees** Delivery charges, service fees, and minimum‑order requirements can add up. Compare total cost across platforms before deciding. 5. **Plan Ahead for Special Orders** For large cakes or intricate designs, place the order at least 48–72 hours in advance. Some bakers require a deposit. ### Where to Start - **Google Maps** – Type “cake delivery near me” or “local bakery” and filter by rating. - **Yelp** – Read recent reviews and see photos. - **Facebook Marketplace** – Many local bakers post their products here. - **Instagram** – Search hashtags like #localbakery, #customcakes, or your city’s name + “bakery.” If you let me know your city or zip code, I can pull up a few highly rated local bakeries and their contact info right now!
